subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-BILLS   MARRIAGE (PROHIBITED DEGREES) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
that Bill S-14, an act respecting the laws prohibiting marriage between related persons, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to move second reading of Bill S-14, an act respecting the laws prohibiting marriage between related persons. A bill like this one was entered for discussion in the 33rd Parliament. It died on the Order Paper.
This present bill is about the third or fourth attempt by this House and by Parliament to make changes to the Marriage Act. Up to this point they have been unsuccessful. It is certainly my hope that the House moves expeditiously on this, agrees to second reading and refers this matter to a legislative committee.
Marriage and divorce are subjects given to the federal Parliament under the British North America Act. It is one of the enumerated heads in that constitutional document. As such it is within the capacity and indeed the responsibility of Parliament to have a look at this particular piece of legislation and, if it deems it necessary, to bring it into conformity with some of our present day thoughts on the subject of marriage.
Turning to a bit of background on this subject, it has always been a part of Judaeo-Christian ethic that there have been and should be some prohibited grounds upon which one person may not marry another based on blood relationships or relationships by marriage. Indeed there are prohibitions in the Old Testament, but the present law we are dealing with had its origins in or about 1563, in the reign of Henry VIII, a man who had more than a passing interest in the subject of marriage. His government tabled a set of prohibitions on whom a person could marry. Basically that table, which found its way into the Anglican Book of Common Prayer, has found its

Private Members' Business
way down to the present time. It was adopted by the common law provinces at the time of Confederation. There were some slight modifications in the province of Quebec, but that is the law that we have today.
I think most people who would have a look at this would agree that changes should be made and that sometimes inequities have resulted because of the fact that this particular act has not been changed.
For instance, if a woman divorced her husband she would not be able to marry her ex-husband's uncle, or indeed she could be prohibited from marrying her ex-husband's uncle by marriage. It does not happen very often, but it does happen in Canada that this creates a hardship on individuals. There are individuals who have got together over the years. There is nothing stopping them from living together; nothing stopping them from having children. There is no law that prohibits that. Yet, sometimes when they have explored their family histories they find this connection.
What do they do about it when they have found it? The process has been to petition the Senate and introduce a Private Member's Bill to correct the problem. Needless to say, this can be time consuming. It is a source of frustration and embarrassment and, because a lawyer is usually employed to get through this process, it can be quite expensive. I think there are good reasons why Parliament should make changes.
I was associated with this bill when it was introduced in the 33rd Parliament. The bill in no way affects or attempts to affect a religion's right to have a prohibited list. It does not in any way compromise a particular religious group's ability to say who can or cannot get married within its fold. This strictly deals with our civil responsibilities. It does not affect the religious responsibilities.
For those who follow this piece of legislation, there is one important change from Bill S-5, which was the legislation introduced in the 33rd Parliament. Bill S-5 did allow marriages between adopted siblings. It prohibited marriages between natural siblings, brothers and sisters, but if a person was related by adoption the old law allowed that. I disagreed with that at the time. I had very serious reservations about it. A number of provinces
had problems with that as well, because the whole thrust of provincial legislation in the area of adoption is to put adopted siblings, as much as possible, on an equal footing. This potential step by a federal Parliament was a step in the wrong direction in their minds and in mine as well.
I am very pleased that this particular legislation referred to us from the other place now prohibits marriage between adopted siblings. With that said, I hope we move expeditiously on this matter. There are Canadians who are waiting for this legislation.
The Senate is not proceeding with Private Members' Business. It is not proceeding with anything, one might say, at the present time. It is definitely not proceeding with petitions in this area of marriage, so I hope this House will deal expeditiously with this bill and send it to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to follow up the remarks of the hon. parliamentary secretary with regard to Bill S-14, to follow the line of thinking he presented to the House, and to offer my support to his position.
I would also like to reiterate that amendments to the Marriage Act are long overdue. For the same reasons as those of the hon. member, Bill S-14 is a better bill than the former Bill S-5. For the same reason that he put forward we now have amendments with regard to adoptive siblings and relationships between adopted children and adopting parents. We have a bill that is more in line with the requirements and the thinking of the provinces and of the population in general.
Now that we have the amendments and the bill in a form acceptable to the House and to the Canadian people, it will solve problems for a great many Canadians who have been waiting a long time for these matters to be straightened out. I think it is in the interest of these people and the country to move ahead quickly with this bill.
The Senate at the present time has 30 Private Members' Bills awaiting it dealing with people who want to get married but who, under the existing act, are prohibited from doing so without the approval of the Senate. The Senate feels very strongly that these changes should be made. It feels that in dealing with Private Members'
October 15, 1990

Bills it is only dealing with something that should be placed and corrected in the legislation itself, and I agree.
It is an embarrassment for these people to have to go through this ordeal and to present themselves before the Senate to air their particular concerns and situations before that august body in the other place. As the parliamentary secretary has said there is a legal cost to these people. I think we should be moving quickly on this matter.
I agree with the parliamentary secretary that this bill should be sent to a legislative committee. Even though we have it in an amended form, which is preferable to the former bill we were discussing, Bill S-5, I think enough time has transpired since we last heard testimony concerning this bill that we should hear some commentary from interested groups and people who have participated in this debate.
Certainly we welcome any of the senators who wish to come forward. We are not interested in having the whole Senate. I am sure it is busy with other things. Its timetable is quite full, but there are three senators in particular, Senator Neiman, Senator Stanbury and Senator Nurgitz who have done a great deal of work on this bill. We owe them a great deal of thanks. At this point I think we should refer the bill to a legislative committee to deal with expeditiously. Then it can be brought back to the House for third reading as quickly as possible so that we can get this piece of legislation through.

There are a lot of groans around the House. Of course, that would never happen.
What does the bill do? The bill reaffirms the law that persons may not marry if they are related lineally or if they are brothers and sisters. It does not change that law. That is a fairly fundamental law that goes back way beyond the times of this Parliament.
However, this law relaxes the law to allow marriage between persons who are related as uncle, niece, aunt and nephew. There are some particular situations where such marriages can come about.
It clarifies the law by providing that a person whose marriage has been dissolved by divorce may many the brother, sister, nephew or niece, et cetera of the divorced spouse. This is not now permitted under the law.
Where has the bill been? The bill is in its third run through this process, as I have already mentioned. It was passed by the Senate in 1986 but died when the House prorogued in October of that year. It was passed again by the Senate but died in the general election of 1988. In fact, the House debated it at second reading in June of 1987.
All the speakers in the debate supported it. The subject matter was referred to a committee of the House which held hearings. I had the pleasure to be at one or two meetings of that legislative committee. However, the subject matter, that is this bill died on the Order Paper with the 1988 general election. There have been extensive Senate hearings into the issue as well as two House of Commons committee meetings.
Over 19 different religious groups, respected family law experts, geneticists as well as the chief law officers of the provinces have been consulted. It is clear that the legislation has had a substantial hearing.
Why should it be passed quickly? I am told that, at present, there are 30 couples requesting the Senate to pass special bills allowing them to marry. You see, Mr. Speaker, you can go before the Senate and get a special bill. Of course, that costs a lot of money and takes a lot of time. Also, it would be pretty difficult to go before the Senate to get things passed right now.
The alternative to this bill would be 30 individual bills. I do not think that is acceptable, because each couple would have to hire a lawyer and go through a long and expensive process with no guarantee of success. I think

October 15, 1990
Private Members' Business
this bill is a reasonable and fair alternative. Besides, I think that this matter is really the domain of Parliament itself.
Let me put it another way. Is this really the domain of Parliament? Perhaps Parliament should not be interfering with couples' choices in this matter. As the senators have noted, the Senate was once in the business of granting divorces. Everybody is happy that the hon. senators are now out of that business.
I must say it was through a lot of work by my predecessors here in the NDP-I can think of Arnold Peters and Frank Howard-who actually filibustered and caused all sorts of embarrassment on these divorce matters. Finally, the government said, well, to heck, we'll pass the new divorce act and get divorce into the courts and out of Parliament. The Senate was once in the business of granting divorces and everyone is happy that the hon. senators have finished. I will end there.
I would like to split my time with my friend from Regina-Lumsden, who is much senior and wiser than me. I believe he had a private members' bill on this subject matter. It is a wonderful thing about the House of Commons, if you hang around long enough, eventually the stuff you have done becomes law. He is not bashful, so I am sure he can speak for himself.
I ask that the hon. member for Regina-Lumsden be allowed the floor to complete the time allotted to our party.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the House for its consent.
I must admit at the outset that I did not hear about this bill until half an hour ago. When I did I had to recall that in the early or mid-70s I had a private member's public bill passed, starting in the Senate, completed in the House of Commons, that made legal the marriage of an uncle to a niece. They had been living together in sin, as
some people would call it, for a number of years. They had two beautiful healthy children, a nice home, he had a good job, they were respected in the community and extremely active in their church.
He wrote to me asking if I could do something for him. I made inquiries of the legal officers of the House and of the Department of Justice. They said the only way it could be done was by an act of Parliament, which would provide for an exception in the current law. On making further inquiries I found out it was going to cost quite a bit of money, especially if you started the bill in the House of Commons. It turned out it would be a lot cheaper to start the bill in the Senate, which is a cheap place to start.
This couple, who emigrated to Canada from the midwest United States, were married in a church twice, but there was no legal recognition of that marriage in the United States. They emigrated to Canada, I think, partly because of that, to try again. They became Canadian citizens and were good citizens. They made a good contribution to society in and around Regina. In fact, he was a leader in the whole business of houses that were environmentally sound and energy efficient.
I mentioned two children and they were beautiful children. But we had to arrange for them to receive several medical examinations. It was declared that they were perfectly normal and fit. Subsequent to that, the aspiring husband obtained a vasectomy.
When the bill came before the House of Commons, we worried about the cost of hiring a lawyer, the air fares for the couple to come to Ottawa, and a lot of other costs. On further inquiry it turned out all one had to do was have a lawyer in Regina draw up the appropriate documents and anyone could appear on behalf of the couple, or they could appear on their own behalf, before the senate committee.
In order to save money the poor couple had me appear on their behalf before the senate committee. I did not ruin the case because the Senate approved it. I might say the committee and the Senate as a whole approved it unanimously.
When the bill appeared before the House of Commons there was a very brief debate and because I made interventions with other members it passed unanimously-

Mr. Speaker, I submit that the law is sufficient as it now stands. The only exception that can occur is when it is provided by Parliament and those have to be circumstances which legally protect the children and any estate that may be left to those children. If for no other reason I submit the law should stand as is because there are exceptions to every rule and to every law and in this kind of instance Parliament should rule about the exception.
I invite hon. members to go back and find the record- I did not have time to look it up myself-and all that was said and done on that occasion.

Mr. Speaker, the Soviet Union has come a long way from the dark days of the cold war when Soviet military power and a Communist dictatorship repressed its people and threatened global security abroad.
Today the 1990 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Mikhail Gorbachev for his phenomenal work in bringing an end to the cold war and drastically reducing the threat of nuclear war. While the world looked on with scepticism, intrigue, hope and finally belief that the impossible was happening, Mikhail Gorbachev, by counselling, negotiation and reassurance has led the Soviet Union to a new place in the international community and the United Nations.
Mr. Speaker, 1990 will be noted by historians as the year when east-west friendship has freed the best and brightest minds in the international community to solve the pressing environmental, social and political problems which no longer take a back seat to the cold war. Mr. Gorbachev deserves the credit he has been given today for helping to bring about this new reality.

Mr. Speaker, for many years the drug Methotrexate has been on the market as a valuable treatment for some forms of cancer.
While on the drug, some people noted that their arthritic problems improved considerably. It was found in further studies that the drug was an effective treatment for arthritis at a much lower dose than used in cancer therapy.
The company involved is now marketing the drug with a new name, Rhematrix, at four times the price of Methotrexate, even though there is no change in the manufacture of the drug. Methotrexate itself is no longer available to the public except through hospital pharmacies.
I would ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to investigate this situation and make sure that the Canadian public is not being ripped off by this marketing change by a major drug firm.

Mr. Speaker, I want to pay tribute today to Lieutenant John van Nostrand from the village of Vandorf who is serving on the HMCS Athabaskan, which is now stationed in the Persian Gulf off Bar Bahrain just 200 miles from Kuwait.
I met with John's mother, Janet, yesterday. She and her husband, Peter, spoke to John by telephone on Sunday, September 30. John was in good spirits, morale is high, and John, who is an engineer, said the HMCS Athabaskan is functioning well. John, who is 29 years old, has been in the Canadian Navy for almost five years. He

October 15, 1990
is a fifth generation van Nostrand from the village of Vandorf where I live.
On behalf of all members of this House, I want to salute all of our Canadian men and women who have joined forces with many other countries to bring peace to this volatile part of the world. We humbly pray for the safe return of all these brave men and women.

Mr. Speaker, the Nobel committee announced today that the 1990 Nobel Peace Prize has been awarded to Soviet President Mikhail Sergeiev Gorbachev for his leading role in the peace process which today characterizes important parts of the international community.
President Gorbachev has demonstrated exceptional leadership in bringing about democratic change in eastern Europe and in the Soviet Union. This fundamental transformation of the region has taken place through a predominantly peaceful process which certainly represents one of his most remarkable accomplishments.

The president is convinced of the need for international security and co-operation. As a result, it was possible to make tangible progress in negotiations on arms control and disarmament between the superpowers.
Mikhail Gorbachev faces many challenges. Today, however, we pay tribute to him for his role in promoting peace and democratic change in Europe.

Let us join in congratulating President Gorbachev and support fully his work toward glasnost and perestroika.

Mr. Speaker, last Saturday noon a group of Canadians, mostly of Palestinian heritage or background, was staging a protest march in the rain protesting the excessive violence to which the Israeli army subjected the Palestinians, and there were 19 deaths.

As in the past, they now appeal to the government of Canada, seeking protection for the human rights of Palestinians under the control of the army of a foreign country.

I would like to suggest to those Canadians of Palestinian heritage, and to all those who plead for human rights and human treatment, to call upon the Canadian Jewish Congress for its help, for I am sure its influence with the Canadian Government would be much more effective.
These people, more than any other, know about suffering, anxiety and fear. I am sure they are aware that something has gone awry in Israel. They can question, with authority, some of the events that have happened in the past few months.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, educational opportunity is a major contributor to personal growth, social mobility, and a vital ingredient of economic growth and international competitiveness.
Today, however, more and more Canadians have begun to question the success of Canada's educational system.
In 1986-87 our primary and secondary educational system in Canada is said to have cost $23.5 billion. Yet, despite the expenditures, the results are mixed at best. In too many cases graduates still have problems with basic literacy and numeracy skills. We have a national dropout rate of 30 per cent, and we have serious skills shortages in Canada.
The time has come to revisit and re-evaluate our educational results. We need a system more sensitive to the future demands of our economy. Failure to do so risks Canada's future social and economic progress.
Education must become a more positive contributor, and our federal government must be a positive contributor in an improved educational process of the future.
October 15, 1990

Mr. Speaker, today in Sudbury Canada Post has closed Postal Station A in New Sudbury to public counter service and will now serve only a small number of commercial customers, leaving the vast number of the public to go to some small private operation. They are now offered reduced service at inadequate outlets. Hopefully they will be able to have their needs met, but in this time before Christmas I doubt it very much.
This is yet another example of Canada Post putting profits before people. As the government continues to carry out its secret plan to privatize all postal services, Canadians are suffering from reduced services and higher prices.
I call upon the minister responsible for the post office to restore the service mandate of Canada Post, to put people before profits, and to restore full service to Postal Station A in Sudbury.

Mr. Speaker, the United States Customs Department has begun a program of nickel and diming Canadian businesses out of the U.S. marketplace by increasing the merchandise processing fee for Canadian businesses exporting into its country.
Effective October 1, 1990, the minimum charge for processing formal entries has risen from $3 to $16.80, an increase of over 500 per cent. Informal entry fees have increased as well. Needless to say, this imposes a severe handicap to our exporters.
The Canadian government must take action immediately to remove this new non-tariff barrier so that Canadian companies presently trading, and those looking to gain access to the U.S. marketplace, will be able to do so free of this restriction.

Liberal senators. President Ghislain Dufour said the Liberal senators had put on a very poor show, in addition to flouting the legitimacy of Parliament and the democratic principles that form the basis for our parliamentary system.

Mr. Speaker, last Thursday I had the pleasure of attending the first Annual Aboriginal Honour Celebration banquet sponsored by the Indian-Metis Friendship Centre of Winnipeg, an evening designed to recognize the major role that aboriginal people have played in the development of Manitoba and the particular achievements of those 12 chosen to be honoured by their community.
Unfortunately, four of the awards had to be given posthumously, like the one for Jackson Beardy in the Arts category, or the one for Tommy Prince, Canada's most decorated war veteran. But others like Dorothy Betz and Mary Richard were there to be duly honoured for their work in the justice system and community development respectively. Dave Courchene, Sr., former chief of Sagkeeng or the Fort Alexander Reserve, was honoured for his pioneer work in aboriginal politics.
The list of accomplished and dedicated aboriginal Canadians is long indeed. Many more such banquets will have to be held to honour them all. But at least a start has been made in Manitoba this last week. All those who made it possible are to be commended.

Mr. Speaker, in 1894 the Lac Seul Indian Band in northwestern Ontario entered into an agreement with the federal government and the province of Ontario. The terms of that agreement have never been respected by the governments involved, which has led the band to submit a land claim under the specific land claims policy of the Department of Indian Affairs.
For more than 20 years now the Lac Seul Band has been working on this particular land claim. Finally, in 1985 it submitted a statement of claim. Five years have since gone by and the Department of Indian Affairs has yet to respond to the claim.
This is just one example of how the government's specific land claims policy works or, for that matter, does not work. We have seen how frustrated the aboriginal community is with this particular policy. The Indian leadership is desperately trying to work with the government on these matters, but one very important element is lacking-trust.
I urge the government to move quickly in revamping its specific land claims policy and do so in consultation with the aboriginal people. The government must seek to regain the trust it has lost and it must live up to its fiduciary responsibilities. Anything less is unacceptable. Action, not meaningless words, is in order.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, Sunday morning at 7.45, it was a farmer from Portage who phoned me and said: "Felix, Mazan-kowski is really listening to us". By announcing interest-free advance payments for grain this weekend, our agriculture minister has proven once again that this federal government is on the side of farmers.
Conservatives have acted. Westerners beware that the Reform Party and Preston Manning are against agricultural support when it is needed the most. The Reform Party would throw Canadian farmers to the wolves of the European Community and the United States.
For a good number of western farmers, interest-free cash advances will mean the difference between putting in a crop or leaving the land. Reform Party ideology would abandon the land and starve the very farmers who built the west.
It is time for western farmers to speak up. It is time for Preston Manning to reform his own platform, or it is time for Preston Manning to sit down and learn that words alone do not put bread on the tables of western farmers and their children.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to inform the House that my provincial New Democrat colleague, Evelyn Gigantes, the Ontario Minister of Health, today helped launch AIDS Awareness Week.
This week's theme is outliving, outloving and outlasting AIDS. In Canada we have identified more than 4,400 AIDS cases, and there are now more than 2,500 Canadians living with AIDS.
There are continuing signs of the spread of the HIV virus, pointing to the need for increased awareness and education, yet there are serious shortcomings in the national AIDS strategy. An all-party committee on AIDS made useful recommendations which have not been acted upon.
What really is needed in AIDS Awareness Week is an awareness by this federal government that it is not meeting the AIDS challenge. We need more research. We need more education and more supportive and improved treatment if we are to eradicate AIDS.

Mr. Speaker, the GST statements, are they fact or fiction? While millions of Canadians oppose the tax, the government clings to this proposed fiscal initiative that will fuel inflation and push us deeper into a recession. That is fact.
In the government's zealous multimillion dollar GST campaign, the spoken word differs from the written word. Here is the fiction. Grocery store owners were

advised in their Revenue Canada GST guide that basic groceries do not include FST and are therefore not eligible for rebate.
Yet on Friday the Minister of Finance stated that there is FST on food. He said it amounts to one or two percentage points.
To meet the government's own objectives, business has been told one thing and consumers are told something totally opposite. Canadians cannot accept this two-faced approach.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are anxiously and optimistically awaiting the introduction of the government's Green Plan.
This is especially so in the case of the people in my riding of Fraser Valley East. The people of the valley from Abbotsford, Chilliwack, Agassiz, Hope and beyond are particularly concerned with air quality. You see, as beautiful as the valley is, as majestic as the mountains may be, the air we breathe leaves much to be desired.
We in the valley are subjected to the smog and emissions of Vancouver. It is literally an ill wind that blows into the valley from the city. The country living of the valley is tainted by the smog of the city, obviously not the best of both worlds.
It is only natural that we in the Fraser valley are anxious about the Green Plan and active solutions. In fact, we are waiting with bated breath. I trust the Minister of the Environment and his colleagues are addressing this problem.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Minister of Finance.
Last week he and the Prime Minister refused to admit there was a recession, but the Prime Minister did agree

that he and his government had induced a slowdown, one planned in the budget of February 1990.
In that budget the Minister of Finance said: "Growth is expected to rebound in the latter half of 1990." We are now in the latter half of 1990, and growth is hardly rebounding. There is less and less growth while there is more and more unemployment.
Does the Minister of Finance still stand by that budget projection on growth? If he does, how is he credible in light of figures showing growing unemployment, growing bankruptcies and the figures today showing a drastic decline in the sale of homes in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I gave a speech on September 17 in Edmonton which gave Canadians the most up-to-date thinking on the part of the government regarding the economy.
In that speech, I said that some of the statements I had made in the budget did not come to pass as quickly as we thought they would. In other words, I expected a weaker economy earlier in the year. The economy was stronger earlier in the year.
The economy is weaker at this time of year, but we expect the recovery to occur as we move into 1991. Economies are vibrant animals. They do not just happen in a static way. We give our best projections at the time.
If my hon. friend would go back to the economic projection record of this government over the last six years, I think he would find that it was enormously better than that of the previous government.

We would also like to be associated with the remarks sent by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the Government of Egypt.
Clearly this is something that every Canadian finds repugnant, as it brings home more clearly that politics is an uncertain business in Canada and is a dangerous business in other parts of the world.
We recognize that for many of the people who take on public office in that region it is a matter of enormous commitment and of some real risk. We hope that some solution can be found to these perilous times in that very difficult region. We hope that this event, if there is anything to come out of it, might provide some reminder of just how important it is that peace be found.

Routine Proceedings PETITIONS

Mr. Speaker, I rise to present a petition, in accordance with Standing Order 36, which has been duly certified by the clerk. It is from 35 of my constituents from the area of Catalina, Bonavista, Port Union, Little Catalina, Melrose, and Elliston.
This petition is concerned about the extra four weeks that people in Newfoundland have to qualify for unemployment insurance. They are very concerned that they will not qualify as the rule stands right now.
I have well over 3,000 in my riding who are concerned about this matter. I was in Catalina and Bonavista this past weekend and the number of people who came to me was well in advance of the 35 who have signed here.
They are concerned that the unemployment rate in Newfoundland is of the highest order in the country. They humbly pray that the variable entrance requirements will be introduced, which would reduce their qualifying time for UIC from 14 weeks to 10 weeks.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today, under Standing Order 36, to present a petition signed by 1,784 residents of Winnipeg North. The petitioners object to the closure of postal services at the Chapman Pharmacy. They point out that the Chapman Pharmacy is conveniently located at a major intersection in Winnipeg, offers optimally convenient hours for residents of the surrounding areas, and has a surrounding community that consists of many seniors and lower-income Canadians who rely heavily on nearby services including the complete range of services provided by this pharmacy.
Moreover, no adequate consultation with this pharmacy was done, and the shortest possible notice was given. Even the month chosen to give notice was one during which the House of Commons was in recess; hence the concerns of the pharmacists and their customers could
not be voiced in Parliament in time. Indeed this postal service outlet has served the community for many decades.
Hence, the petitioners ask Parliament to do all it can in order for the minister responsible for Canada Post Corporation to reconsider the decision taken by this corporation to close postal services at the Chapman Pharmacy, in the interest of fairness to the Chapman Pharmacy and in recognition of the excellent postal services it has rendered to its many customers who stand to suffer should the closure persist. Therefore, the petitioners seek remedy in this House.

Mr. Speaker, I too have the honour of presenting petitions on behalf of Canadians, pursuant to Standing Order 36.
The residents of Canada who signed this petition state that the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child protects children's human rights in such key areas as adoption, survival, development, protection of the child's identity, sexual exploitation, neglect, and drug abuse.
The petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to urge strongly the federal government to encourage universal adherence to the UN Convention of the Rights of the Child and prompt an effective implementation of its provisions.
The petitioners ask the federal government to review its legislation and policies for consistency with the convention.

That this House condemn this government for planning and

He said: Mr. Speaker, I think it is important to establish from the outset that this govemement planned and implemented a recession whose existence is recognized by practically all Canadians.
In the past few weeks, the minister said repeatedly that in his February Budget he projected data that clearly showed we would be Ain a slowdown-to use the minister's words-that the unemployment rate would increase and that the country's economic growth rate would drop or disappear altogether. This means, Mr. Speaker-and this is very a very important point-that, as we said in our motion, the government indeed planned and implemented this recession.
What Canadians deplore, however, is the fact that the Minister of Finance apparently cannot accept that his planning led to the results desired by this government-a recession, in other words.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that in this debate, it would be important to hear the Minister of Finance agree, once and for all, and this would at least be a start towards solving the problem, that Canada is indeed in a full-fledged recession.
We need only listen to the comments of all partners in our economy. We could ask about inflation in Quebec: what inflation? The Minister of Finance steadfastly refuses to accept there is such a thing, although we are aware of it and its existence has been recognized, for instance, by the Conference Board of Canada, the Mouvement Desjardins, the National Bank of Canada and a wide range of representatives from the business
Supply
community, labour, consumers and by Canadians in general.

Mr. Speaker, what we believe Canadians are more concerned about than anything else at this point, recognizing that there is very little that individual Canadians and even corporations can do about the recession in which we find ourselves, is the refusal of the minister to recognize the fact that we are, in fact, in a recession and, as our motion states, it is a made-in-Canada recession.
I listened with great interest to the comments of the Minister of Finance during Question Period, when he said such things as "cast your mind back to 1981-82" and commented on the high rates of interest and the high rates of inflation that Canada was experiencing at that time.
The Minister of Finance knows well that it was a phenomenon that was rampant throughout the western world. We had situations in the United States and in western Europe where inflation and interest rates were going through the roof.
The Minister of Finance pointed out to the Leader of the Opposition that there was a discrepancy in the position taken by the Leader of the Opposition, in his capacity then as a member of the government, and what he is saying now. I would like to point out that it is awful dangerous, as I am sure the Minister of Finance is aware, to comment on what was said 10 years ago, when the Minister of Finance was occupying a somewhat different position himself at that point in time.
But I did not make that type of comment.

Let me quote the Minister of Finance in 1984. He said this: "What we remember most about that period", speaking about the early eighties, "is the fact that interest rates were far higher than they should have been. Interest rates skyrocketed during that period to between 22 per cent and 25 per cent. The reason was largely because of what went on in the United States and the very high interest rate policy followed there".
Mr. Speaker, this is what Canadians are getting extremely upset about. It is that we do not seem, as politicians, regardless of which side of the House we sit on, to remember what we said not all that long ago. We are very quick to point out some conflicts perhaps in

positions taken by members of the Opposition but very slow to accept what the Minister of Finance and others were saying at that point.
In that same speech in this place, in 1984, the Minister of Finance, speaking then as the financial critic for the Opposition, stated that the 1981 budget raised taxes just at the point when the economy was falling into recession and we should have been reducing taxes.
I wonder what the Minister of Finance thinks about that formula now, as he continues to berate the Senate for being very careful about the implementation of the goods and services tax. Most observers recognize it will take a pretty substantial amount of money out of the Canadian economy at a time when we are going to be in a recession.
The Minister of Finance says we are wrong. I listen to him in this House and in his speeches in Edmonton and other places, when he suggests that the GST bill must come out of the Senate because it is fundamental to his deficit-reduction program and it is fundamental to the government's revenue-generation plan.
Again, relating to the comments made by the Minister of Finance when he was finance critic in 1984, referring to the recession that we had experienced in the early eighties, he said: "We were helpless, as we watched the United States rates climb higher and higher. Canadian rates followed".
Mr. Speaker, that is the point. Canadian rates are not following now, Canadian rates are four and five points above the American base rate. It is an historical situation to see that much of a margin between Canadian and American rates. Yet, the Minister of Finance insists on casting our minds back-he talks about dying before we get to heaven, and so forth-and asks the question as to why the members of the Opposition support the Senate in its fight against the goods and services tax.
I want to point out to the Minister of Finance that the reason Canadians and members of the opposition support the Senate in this fight against the goods and services tax is because they know the senators who are fighting the tax are right. It is not very complicated.
It is one thing to be selective and to suggest that big brother is right and they are always correct, when in fact, if we go back to the budget wherein the minister set out
his pattern that could lead into a recession, because he was half right, he said that unemployment would go up and growth would slow or else disappear. But he also said that interest rates were going to come down significantly and would average on the calendar year 11.1 per cent.
We were dead wrong on that. As everybody in the country knows, interest rates over this year will be significantly higher than what was projected in the budget.
One could think that perhaps the opposition is guilty of overstating the case, that after five years-because the Minister of Finance celebrated his anniversary in Edmonton, I understand when he made his speech on September 17, and it was six years-you would think, Mr. Speaker, that after six years, the minister would recognize that even friends of the government, people who were extremely vocal in 1988 with respect to the government's performance to that point and what they had projected for free trade, had come out and stated that they are concerned about the economic mismanagement. This is not the Liberal Party of Canada talking about what is happening to our economy.
I quote from the joint statement on the national economy made October 11 by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce and the Business Council on National Issues. They state, "We wish to underline the growing concern within the Canadian business community that domestic macroeconomic mismanagement, persistent fiscal laxity and a failure to come to grips with the magnitude of the competitiveness challenge confronting Canadian industry are steadily undermining Canadians' economic prospects".
We could go on at length and join the chorus of boos across the country with respect to the government's performance on the economy, but I do not think that that serves any useful purpose because it has all been said. Canadians are aware that when people are confronted with problems in their personal life, in their business life, whatever the case might be, the first step toward trying to correct the difficulty or the problem is to recognize it.
I believe that what Canadians want from the Minister of Finance and from the Prime Minister are not statements that this economic slowdown is healthy or that

things are going according to plan. They want to knows specifically first of all, does the government recognize that the kinds of projections that are involved in budget documents, and the kinds of assessments that are made in speeches on the state of the Canadian economy do not reflect the human suffering that is going on in the country, when bankruptcies are at very, very high levels across the country, when unemployment is increasing, when housing starts are down and people generally are discouraged. It is not just the fact that they are faced with that we are in a recession, it is the seeming inability of the government to understand the depth of the problem.
I hope, as we pursue this debate today, that we will have provided the Minister of Finance with an opportunity to discuss the interest policy, to tell us why in 1990 we should be leading the way for Americans in showing them where they can invest their money at extremely high levels of interest, why we are killing our export industry. We talk on the one hand about correcting the difficulty with the manufacturers' sales tax, when in fact the high value of the Canadian dollar is doing more damage to Canadian exports than the FST or the MST has ever done, even taking into account that the government has increased the federal sales tax from 9 to 13.5 per cent in the five and half to six years they have been in power.
I hope we will be able to hear from the Minister of Finance today. What Canadians are looking for is first, does the government and the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance accept the fact that we are in a real recession. It is not a question of technical recession. Looking at the number of jobs that we are losing across the country and the increasing rate of unemployment, can we get a clear, categorical statement from the government, through the Minister of Finance, that yes, we are in a recession. Then can we begin to deal with it in the life of that reality.
The difficulty of trying to deal with any problem in Canada as a politician today is a major challenge. We have heard a great deal of what is going on in the other place. I know that the Minister of Finance and other members of government on a regular basis discuss the bills that are before the members of the other place.

They ask Canadians to try and force the issue to make sure the goods and services tax passes.
When we went across the country with the Standing Committee on Finance of the House of Commons, we met many people who, in various ways, were very calm, logical and rational in their presentations. Others were extremely upset and very aggressive in their rejection of the goods and services tax. I am sure the same experience occurred for members of the Senate when they went across the country and met with Canadians in discussing the goods and services tax.
To put things in perspective, when people are facing a made-in-Canada recession-most of the time we like to have little stickers on things saying, made in Canada, we are proud of it, we have put the red flag on it and we have logos to indicate that particular products are made in Canada. I do not think anyone is very proud of the fact that we have a made-in-Canada recession.
People are frustrated as we enter this recession. Many sectors of the economy and parts of the country have been in a recession for some time. It is not something that happened last week when the Conference Board of Canada came out with its report. I see headlines in the press over the weekend saying: "Racket emanates at anti-GST rally" and noisemakers and so on. Although some people have had some reservations about some of the approaches taken by senators at specific times in their fight against the GST, I believe that in the context of what people have to face in the real world, they understand the frustration of the senators.
On the weekend I had the occasion to speak with literally hundreds of people. Not one person said, "Tell the senators to pass the GST." Some people had some comments about some of the goings on in the other place but no one said, "Make sure when you get back to Ottawa that you tell those people in the other place to pass the goods and services tax." One of the things we have to understand is that the members of the Liberal Party who sit in the Senate are very much aware that what they had done in that place will in fact require that Senate reform take place.

I would hope as we go through this debate that we will hear from the Minister of Finance. There is no doubt that it has given up the battle on this. There is not question as it relates to the goods and services tax or management of the economy in general, that the government has taken the John Paul Jones approach of damn the torpedoes and full speed ahead, and we are going to do it regardless.
I know the Minister of Finance has held that office almost longer than any finance minister in the history of this country. Whether or not he has decided to go down with the ship is something we are going to learn in the very near future. It is important for Canadians to feel that the Minister of Finance understands their problems. Second, it is important for Canadians to believe that the Minister of Finance and the government will respond to those problems. We believe that the government has to bring in a revised budget, if not a new budget, a mini budget, a new statement. The September 17 statement in Edmonton recognized some of the changes that have occurred in our economy. But the fact is that the projections in the budget the minister brought in in February are completely off base because so much of it is now proven to be erroneous.
It is no longer a question of speculation on interest rates. It is no longer a question of speculation on the amount of the deficit. We are in a different situation and Canadians believe that they have a right to have the finance minister come in. He does not have to say: "Mea culpa," and beat his chest. He just has to say what Canadians already know, that it has not turned out the way we thought it would, and we believe we now have to change. We have to say to the Governor of the Bank of Canada that there has to be a reduction in interest rates and that he is not moving in a long-term way with enough credibility to be able to force the value of the Canadian dollar down to try to protect our export industries.
The other question I want to draw on before I conclude is the argument by the Minister of Finance and government members that there are no alternatives. When the Minister of Finance came before the Canadian people after the 1984 election, he talked about a long-term plan to stabilize the fiscal situation in the country. He talked about tax reform, deficit reduction, and spending restraint.
We are in a far worse situation now than we were in 1984. The minister can say that relatively speaking, and using the right numbers, there have been some improvements. But the fact of the matter is that the debt is far higher, the cost of servicing the debt is far higher, and interest rates are higher than they have ever been in relation to American rates in terms of the separation between the two. What we need to find out today, or very soon, is if the government is prepared to look at alternatives.
When the minister states that there are no alternatives, surely he understands that it is not within the realm of possibility for ordinary Canadians, or even people who have a lot of expertise in the tax field, to come in with a panacea. The minister has been struggling with it for six years.
Neil Brooks of the University of Toronto came out with an alternative suggestion. Dennis Mills of our party has been working at trying to put forward a simple tax proposal. There is another group at the University of Toronto that recently put forward some proposals to deal with the replacement for the goods and services tax. We are not suggesting that any one of these alternatives is the absolute answer.

What we want to continue to impress on the government and the Canadian people is that the Liberal Party believes the only way to have meaningful and credible tax reform is to deal with it on a massive basis through consideration of what the implications are for provincial governments and municipal governments. There is no simple solution of shifting the burden of taxation from one level of government to the other because the taxpayer is always the same.
We believe this is a made-in-Canada recession and that it was planned and put in place by the government. We hope we will have an opportunity to hear from the Minister of Finance who will recognize that we are now in that recession that the government has planned. What we want to hear is how does he intend to get us out of the recession.

The answer is 6.1 per cent on average over the last six years and the program spending for the Government of Canada-in other words, its own spending-is 3.7 per cent. So the transfer to the provinces have been considerably greater than what we have spent on all other things in the Government of Canada.
Since 1984, as my hon. friend knows, we have set forward a very clear plan of economic policy for the country. There are three fundamental issues that we have been following here. One is to deal with the nation's finances-the deficit and the debt problem.
My colleague during his comments said that we were backing away from all the major challenges. I do not see how the hon. member for a minute can say that we have backed away from the major challenges of cutting government spending when we have had to deal with difficult issues such as the closing of bases which is close to his part of the country. It has affected places there. VIA Rail has affected his part of the country-very much so. These are decisions that we do not enjoy taking, but we have not backed away from them.
On the one hand, my hon. friend criticizes me for not getting the deficit down, then on the other hand ignores the very difficult and tough decisions that we have taken in getting the deficit down.
The second area of our economic policy is reducing structural barriers, privatization, deregulation, training for people who are out of work, tax reform, both corporate and personal income tax, and now sales tax reform, and finally, getting the problem of inflation under control. We have made some very clear and very tangible progress here.
The cost of running the government today was $100 million less last year in dollars spent-not inflation adjusted dollars but in dollar spent-than in 1984.
I have talked about our record of controlled program spending. In the operating balance, we came from a $16 billion deficit to a $14 billion surplus this year, a $30 billion turnaround.
Our success here has been greater than the United States. We have moved further in a shorter period of time than the United States has in dealing with their deficit problem. So we have seen a made-in-Canada improvement in our control of our fiscal position. We have also seen a made-in-Canada improvement of the economic capacity of the government because of this range of structural policy changes that are equivalent to $30 billion, or equivalent on an ongoing basis annually to the size of the gross provincial product of the province of Manitoba.
We have debated the GST. We have debated it endlessly in this House. That will put our exporters and importers on a level playing field with the international competition, something that will help us generate jobs here in Canada.
The OECD describes a process we have been following in structural reform as substantial and as noteworthy. The Economic Council of Canada review has also commented very positively on what we have been able to do in dealing with these structural issues.
Now, inflation control. Inflation was a problem. It was getting out of control, but we have brought inflation down, for the seventh consecutive month, to 4.1 per cent. We have real challenges here because the pressures are pretty substantial. As I pointed out, in the United Kingdom they were 10.9 per cent last month. That gives some indication of what happens to a country that does not take its inflation problem seriously.
October 15, 1990

From 1984 to 1989 we had a made-in-Canada growth in this country which was second only to that of Japan. A million and a half new jobs were created by Canadian businesses here. Again, a made-in-Canada boom in this country. The growth that we have seen, the second longest period of continuous growth in the post-war period, has resulted in real benefits to the standard of living of Canadians: from 1983 to the present, a 16 per cent improvement in average per capita income, after inflation, after income taxes. That amounts to an $8,000 improvement in the purchasing power of the average Canadian family.
Credit growth was getting out of hand though, Mr. Speaker. We had credit growth. Consumer credit reached a peak of 15 per cent. In June it was still a 10.2 per cent increase, almost double what it was in the United States.
Business credit growth, again 2 percentage points higher than the United States; mortgage credit growth, 16 per cent in the month of June-that is twice the rate of growth of our economy and about two and a half times the rate of mortgage growth in the United States.
Unit labour costs, one of the best measures of our competitive position, which my hon. friend is concerned about and his colleague from Etobicoke North was concerned about earlier in Question Period. We were seeing an increase in our unit labour costs a good deal higher than the United States and about twice as high as the rate of growth in Germany and Japan. So we needed a firm monetary policy to deal with the problem that we have today.
My hon. friend talked about the problems of 1981-82, saying that they were quite different. In Canada they were the same. The economy was growing more quickly than the capacity of the country to handle, it was for that reason that we had to impose the higher interest rate policy in Canada, to deal with this Canadian problem. I make no apologies for that.
What we have done, Mr. Speaker, is to be sensitive. We listened very carefully to what is happening in the economy. I know there are tough times out there. I talked to businesses that are closing. I talked to people who have lost their jobs. I take no satisfaction whatsoever in that. But I do know that if we had ignored this problem, the problems we would have faced in six
Supply
months, nine months, a year, two years down the road would have been far more serious, far more disruptive, far more damaging to the prospects of Canadians than is the case right now. We have this problem under control now to a far greater extent than-again, let me remind you-is the case in Great Britain.
We have had made-in-Canada growth. It developed into a made-in-Canada problem so we imposed a made-in-Canada solution so we can have made-in-Canada strong non-inflationary growth into the future. This is what my hon. friend, my hon. colleague from the Liberal Party is asking for, a policy response and a clear sense of direction to Canadians as to the policies that we are following and where this is going to take us as a country.
What I find very difficult to accept, Mr. Speaker, is the continued allegations on the other side that we could have a reduction in interest rates just by snapping our fingers.
These people should listen to what the Economic Council or what the three business groups that my hon. friend referred to just a minute ago said. They said: "The only way you are going to get interest rates down is to control government spending, not just the Government of Canada, but all governments because all governments are part of this problem." That is a clear message that came out from the business groups last week.
My friend is selectively ignoring these words. He is selectively ignoring the proposals, the prescriptions that these organizations have come up with. They say: "You have to get the deficit down." You cannot just snap your fingers and hope for lower interest rates. Interest rates will only come down if the circumstances are right to support lower interest rates.
This is where I have the greatest difficulty with the policies of the Liberal Party. It says: "Your fiscal policy is wrong. You should have a lower deficit. You should have lower interest rates." Then, what do we hear from them? We just heard the best example.
There was a vacuous, totally empty response when I asked what the alternatives were. What are the things that the opposition parties are suggesting we should do to get the deficit down to allow us to get the interest rates down? There was an empty response, and my hon. friend knows it. I think he is embarrassed about it, but that is what his leadership has told him to do.

I referred to this in Question Period I referred to, and I repeat it again. The Economic Council did come up with a scenario that said if rates were brought down to our February budget level, the result would be a combination of economic growth and a wiping out of the deficit by 1995. They also pointed out a dark side: "That would be an inflation rate that would be disruptive, causing a return to monetary restraint in the mid-1990s. In short, this is a flight plan for a rollercoaster ride." That is the point that I wanted to make.
We know that the economy is in tough shape. We know that people are going through a difficult period here. The key that we have to ask ourselves is: If we had taken the roller-coaster ride that the Economic Council has described, where would we be in one, two, three or five years time? We are determined not to get into that same trap that was fallen into not just by the government here in Canada, but by governments in other parts of the world as well. That is why we are following these policies.
This takes me to where we are now in the life of this Parliament. This government has put forward four pieces of legislation. Bill C-21 is the unemployment insurance bill. It includes a number of elements of unemployment insurance reform, designed to broaden the scope of unemployment insurance at the same time as tightening up on unemployment insurance, and also providing some financing to the Government of Canada to allow it to get its deficit down.
Bill C-28 is a number of income tax measures, including the large corporations tax. Bill C-69 is a bill designed to reduce a number of government spending programs so that all of these together can take real action to get the deficit under control.
In addition, Bill C-62 is designed to stabilize the fiscal position of the Government of Canada. All of these are designed to do precisely what the Economic Council and these business groups have suggested we do, get the deficit down.
In December 1987 we had a report from the senators. Senator MacEachen, Senator Buckwold, the current chairman of the finance committee, and Senator Kirby, all of those gentlemen are fighting these four bills, as well as the GST.
I believe I have seven more minutes, Mr. Speaker. I started at 3.45 p.m.
Those three senators are fighting the GST and these other bills. Those three senators came in with a report in a Liberal dominated committee which says that they recommend that the government scrap the federal sales tax and introduce a multi-stage, broad based sales tax, which is precisely what the goods and services tax is.
This is the hypocrisy that I see in this place when, on the one hand, we have people like my friend opposite saying: "You should do this." Then, on the other hand, he takes all the steps possible to make it extremely difficult if not impossible to do the things that he is precisely requesting that we do.
The Liberal Party ran in the last election and number two on the Liberal Party election platform was: "A Liberal government will not proceed with stage two of the Mulroney government's tax reform plan". That is the sales tax proposal, that is the GST proposal. The Liberal Party said it would not. The Liberal Party was not elected to form the government. The Conservative Party, under the Prime Minister, was elected to form the government.
Now we have a position where the elected government passed a bill in the House of Commons that was part of the Liberals' election platform to defeat and our election platform to pass. We have passed it, with a majority government supported by Canadians in the last election, and now we have not just the Liberal senators but a minority of the senators in the Senate saying: "No, we are going to rise up out of the past, we senators who were appointed by Mr. Trudeau when he was Prime Minister, and we are going to ignore what the people decided on November 21, 1988". They are going to do what that party which was defeated in that same election would do. They say that they are going to kill that tax, in spite of the fact that they were beaten on that platform.
I appeal to my hon. friend and to other members opposite because we have an important problem here, not only a fiscal problem. We have to get these bills passed to be able to deal with the fiscal position of the Government of Canada, and we have a fundamental, democratic problem here.
I just read from the editorial support here. One reads: "Shame on you Liberal senators". There are references to the Senate as an undemocratic anachronism. Others read: "Time for the deadlock clause"; "elected House must show the Senate who's boss"; "the Prime Minister had little choice"; "an abuse of Senate power, embar-

rassing to all Canadians"; "forget the shameful antics, we need the GST"; "surgery needed to save democracy and the GST"; "the games senators play"; "opinion polls no reason for Senate to stall the GST"; "anarchy in the Senate"; "the Liberals should be ashamed of themselves".
I have many, many more of these, but the answer is very clear: It is fundamentally important for the future of parliamentary democracy in this country that we proceed with this legislation that is being blocked in the Senate by the Liberal minority there. It is an important fiscal problem. Those bills are key to the ability of this government to manage the fiscal position of the Government of Canada.
I have not heard members opposite in the House of Commons who sit on the Liberal side saying why they feel in this day and age that we should have an unelected, appointed, unaccountable group of people who are appointed by a previous government. How can they justify that group of people blocking the will of the people as expressed on November 21, 1988 and as expressed in the platform of the Government of Canada?
The Liberals said they would block this if elected, but they were not elected. If we are going to establish a precedent of having a minority of senators blocking this legislation, I ask my colleagues opposite: Where does that leave us as a country? What recourse do the Canadian people have if they want to have a large corporations tax, if they want to have $500 million more in training programs, if they want to have maternity benefits, and if they want to see senior citizens who are earning more than $50,000 contribute toward lowering the deficit by putting back some or all of their Old Age Security? What recourse do Canadians have? They cannot vote out Allan MacEachen. They cannot vote out Michael Kirby. They cannot vote out Sid Buchwold. They have to wait for those gentlemen to reach age 75. That is not the right way.
People have said to me from other countries when I tell them what is going on here: "This is a joke. It is an anachronism. It is 19th century stuff. I thought we got rid of all this. What is going on? What is the GST?" When I explain it to them they say: "That is the same as our
Supply
value added tax. Why are these unelected Liberal senators saying you should not have a tax we have had it for 20 or 25 years?"
This is the challenge that is facing Canadians and this House today. Are we going to pass this legislation which will help us get the fiscal position of the Government of Canada in a stabilized and normalized position? Are Liberal party members opposite going to continue to be held hostage by their colleagues in the Senate who are not elected?
Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, first of all, on the question of the goods and services tax that allegedly the government party put forward in the last election, as I recall that proposal, even the minister's own technical documents in August of last year indicated that it would be visible, harmonized, fair, and revenue neutral.
I do not think one Canadian voted for the goods and services tax proposal that the minister has brought forward. We will let Canadians debate that, and I am sure they will whenever they have an opportunity.
I have a simple question for the Minister of Finance. The minister asked about alternatives. I indicated in a reply that I thought that what had been proposed by the Standing Committee on Finance in its report last year was a valid contribution to try to turn things around in this country and avoid the recession we are now in.
I want to ask the Minister of Finance if in his widespread consultation he has done the following or, if he has not done so, if he would consider doing it now? Would the minister take the time, along with his officials, to contact the exporters, the manufacturers in Canada, and ask them this question: "Would you rather have the goods and services tax passed or would you rather have a 75-cent to 80-cent Canadian dollar and interest rates at

11 per cent?" I think it would be very interesting to get an answer to that question.
I believe we have the answer because we have been listening to these people. They will have to choose between the two because they will not be able to have both, in that the GST will cause inflation that will not make it possible to drop the interest rate as much as the minister might like. I think it would be very enlightening to ask the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and to ask the pulp and paper industry and the mining industry if they would rather have a 75-cent to 80-cent dollar with interest rates at 11 per cent or the GST.

Mr. Speaker, there is another one of the cute little tactics of the senior finance critic of the Liberal Party. It is not an either/or. No one has ever put it and no one should ever put it as an either/or question if they knew what they were talking about.
We are doing the GST for fundamental reasons because the existing tax is broken, and he knows full well it is. He also knows full well that the exporters, manufacturers, and others in this country on whom we depend for a significant number of jobs, need the GST.
The level of the Canadian dollar and our monetary policy are quite separate from whether or not we have the GST. The monetary policy must be there to deal with the inflationary problem that we have been struggling with over the past two and a half to three years.
My hon. friend referred to the finance committee report of about a year ago. At that time mortgage credit was growing at a rate of 17 per cent; consumer credit was growing at a rate of 12 to 14 per cent per annum; and business credit, 11 per cent, for an economy that was growing at a rate of 7 per cent or 8 per cent.
If he is suggesting that it would have been an appropriate, intelligent, prudent policy of the Governor of the Bank of Canada to lower interest rates at the time when credit demand was booming and suggesting that that would not lead to significantly higher inflation, I think that he is dead wrong. That is exactly what would have happened, and that is why we felt it was important.
I remind him that in August 1988 we had a unanimous recommendation from the provincial premiers to reduce interest rates. If we had done that, at this point in time we would be looking at an inflation rate probably closer to what they have in Great Britain at 10.9 per cent than the level of inflation today.
He says that the tax we promised was visible. I do not know how much more visible this tax could be. I wish it were invisible.
Harmonized, I have always said that it was my first preference to have a harmonized tax. We have the province of Quebec harmonizing with us. We have the province of Saskatchewan in discussions. We have other provinces talking about harmonizing.
Is it fair that the GST credit will reduce the amount of taxes paid by families earning less than $30,000? I believe that means a fair tax.
Revenue neutral, we can debate that one until the cows come home. I have stated very clearly what the position of the Government of Canada is and I stand by that.

Mr. Speaker, my question for the minister is in reference to his claim that only the Liberal opposition seems to be opposed to this insidious measure.
He will no doubt be aware that one of his colleagues stated recently in the newspaper that he had consider crossing the floor on the issue of the GST. I would like to just read a quote into the record: "Our office has never received as many calls and letters nor have I had as many comments burning my ears off about a whole series of issues. While constituents are unhappy about everything from free trade to the Oka crisis, Meech Lake, Prime Minister Brian Mulroney's leadership and recent controversial Senate appointments, the GST remains atop the list".
Oh, oh.

The member for St. John's East yells out "propaganda". If that is propaganda, he should be aware that these were statements made recently in the newspaper by the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth who, the last time I looked, was still a member of the Conservative Party.
I would like to ask the minister what response he has to his colleague who obviously is feeling the heat from
October 15, 1990

his constituents but does not have the guts to take the courage of his convictions and cross the floor to sit as an independent.
He will.

Mr. Speaker, her colleagues from Acadie-Bathurst says that we do not have the courage to meet these major challenges that we are faced with. If the GST is not a major challenge, I do not know what is, but I remind colleagues that for 50 years now, starting with the Rowell-Sirois report in 1940 and every 10 years since then, there have been recommendations to scrap the existing manufacturers' sales tax and bring in a new type of sales tax.
Jean Chretien, when he was Minister of Finance in 1977, observed that the existing sales tax should be changed.
Allan MacEachen brought in a budget in 1981 to change the existing sales tax to the wholesale level. It did not work. He asked Wolfe Goodman of Toronto, one of the pre-eminent commodity tax practitioners in the country to bring in a report. Mr. Goodman brought in the report, as I said around the time of the 1984 election, and it was that report which said: "not at the wholesale level. You have to bring in a tax. To be a properly designed commodity tax, it should be brought in at the retail level".
In response to my friend from Hamilton East, sure, we are all feeling the heat. We all know that this tax is not popular, but colleagues on this side of the House are prepared to tough it out because they know it is the right thing for the country. They know that it is one of the most significant things that we can do to improve the economy of the country and also to put our exporters, people who compete against importers, in a solid position to compete and create jobs. Also it will reduce the cost of new investment in Canada, in the case of Quebec which has harmonized with us by 7.5 per cent, equivalent to a 7.5 per cent invest tax credit.
For someone who represents a steel town, why is my friend resisting a type of tax initiative that will have such a positive impact on the steel industry in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, my question for the Minister of Finance relates to productivity. He is always talking in this House about how the tax system is designed to help
Supply
our exports along and give some incentive to our manufacturers.
When I talk to the people in my city, which the Minister of Finance shares, the biggest disincentive to productivity is the sense of unfairness that exists on the shop floor and executive offices, which in turn goes all the way through the economy.
Does the minister really believe that he can create an environment of world-class productivity, with an environment in business where, forgetting for a moment the GST and all its complications, but just the entire tax system which people do not perceive to be fair and where they do not understand: there are parts of the tax act which are used for jobs, and there are parts of the tax act which are so old that it is just out of touch and out of date. When will the minister open the shop door and start listening to people who really know what productivity is all about and the current environment that he is creating-

How can the Minister of Finance possibly believe that a complicated system like the GST, his entire economic package right now, can do anything to promote productivity or a spirit in our economy that is going to lift us out of this recession we are in?

Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend would agree with me that the GST will remove a hidden burden of tax on all our exporters. That is going to help productivity. It puts Canadian companies on a fair and level playing field with the imports that they have to compete with, whereas now the imports pay one-third less tax. That helps our productivity. Moving to the GST will reduce the cost of new investment by 4 per cent for those provinces that have not harmonized and by 7.5 per cent in the case of Quebec that has harmonized. That is productivity.
I think what the hon. member is getting at is attitudes. My hon. friend has written a book on taxation. He is saying there is a sense of unfairness, and I say to him that he is fostering that sense of unfairness by using statistics
